guages act again and start out, as I said, with a brand new piece of paper. The reality of a country, the reality of a constitution and the realities of people who come together in a country such as Canada, which stretches from sea to sea, is that it is not possible to start out in a vacuum. We Eire bound to go back and see what our roots are; we are bound to go back and see where our people were, where our descendants were, where the graves are. It is necessary to go back to find out where you have populated, where you have prospected and where you have had some dreams. You do not start out in a vacuum. Yet today some hon. members appear to forget so much of our history. I have Irish blood in my veins, and I shall not necessarily wave the Union Jack because some people in Ireland, where my ancestors came from many centuries ago, do not think the Union Jack is all that great.
I am not proselytizing for the Union Jack; I am not proselytizing for the English tongue as compared with the French tongue. I am proselytizing, I am preaching, I am philosophizing about what makes a country tick-and you do not make a country tick when you have one-eyed vision. You do not make a country tick when you have a patch on one eye and then start to go blind in the other. I do not question the motives of any hon. member who has spoken today in this most interesting discussion. It has been a basic exchange. I say in all sincerity that you cannot take a constitution in a vacuum; you cannot start in Canada today and forget about everything in the past; you cannot concentrate on one element only, for example on British subjects, forgetting completely not only the English-speaking people who will one day come to Canada once we pass a law which affects them but the British subjects, the Commonwealth subjects who came to Canada under the law as it stood and as it stands today until we pass a new one.
This question involves fundamental rights, right or wrong; and I suppose there is considerable room for debate there among hon. members. Once we start taking away fundamental rights retroactively, whether they are language rights, voting rights or citizenship rights, we establish in this chamber a precedent which can come back like a boomerang and affect the rights of any minority anywhere in this land. It is for this reason I feel so strongly that many hon. members who are sincere, and who hold their convictions as strongly as I hold mine, are misguided. They

about participation in committees, about members involving themselves in committees and committees holding 14 meetings on Tuesdays and Thursdays, that once a committee has finally reviewed this bill the co-ordinator of committees in the House becomes the hatchetman to cut the guts out of this clause under discussion.
I appreciate that the hon. member has every right in this House, as I have, to make speeches and to move amendments. Retroactive legislation that affects the rights of people is even worse. Clause 14(3) will affect a certain body of people in the land. Whether or not they are citizens is another point. Many of these people have been voting in Canada for up to 50 years, and there may be 500,000 of them. If this bill is passed in its present form, the rights they now have had will be taken away. I say that instead of advancing the cause of unity in this country, this bill will disenfranchise those who have enjoyed the franchise up until now.
I do not want this issue to become confused with the position of newcomers to Canada. I agree that there should not be three or four classes of Canadians given certain privileges, if this can be avoided. There are several classes of Canadians today. For example, we have British subjects who came to Canada and are covered under the old law. Englishspeaking and French-speaking Canadians have certain rights under other laws. Then I admit there is that anomalous group of British subjects who are covered under the existing law. But until Parliament changes the law that applies to newcomers to Canada in the future, it would be a mistake to pass a bill that would disenfranchise and adversely affect the rights of so many Canadians who have enjoyed the franchise heretofore.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think this amendment should be voted on until someone on the government side satisfies me, at least, of its legality. In the next two or three minutes I should like to direct my remarks to the right of the committee to accept an amendment which, in effect, in a legal sense demands the amendment of other law. I am not learned in the law. As a matter of fact, I am not very learned in many matters. But it does seem to me that there is a serious point involved here and I am wondering why the minister who is piloting the legislation through the committee, or for that matter any other member of the government, has not bothered to address himself to it.
Before the question is put, preferably when we reconvene at eight o'clock this evening, it would serve the members of the committee well, as well as assist in the task ahead of us, if the minister during the supper hour would obtain a legal opinion on whether what the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra has proposed is indeed within our capacity to accept.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps I could just satisfy the hon. member in that regard. I advanced an opinion before the dinner hour regarding the extension of the qualification in respect of British subjects other than Canadian citizens, and I might explain that turn of phrase by pointing out that of course under our citizenship act all Canadian ci izens are by definition British subjects. This amendment does not in any way affect that status. The fact that the right to vote is given or withheld under this act does not in any way change their basic status as Canadian citizens. They are required to look to the citizenship act and to their status under it as to whether or not they are Canadian citizens, British subjects or aliens. The giving or wilhholding of the right to vote does not affect that status in any way. By way of analogy I point out that our friend the Chief Electoral Officer is disqualified from voting in an election. The fact that Her Majesty's judges are not entitled to vote in an election does not make them any less Canadian citizens. In a certain number of
limited cases there has been the removal of the qualification to vote, but that does not affect citizenship status.
There is one thing I think it might be worthwhile referring to because the question was inferentially raised by the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek this afternoon. That is whether or not there would be difficulty for someone who is in the situation where he was not born in Canada but is deemed to be a naturalized Canadian by reason of the Canadian Citizenship Act. The question is whether such a person would in any way require proof upon this rather difficult legal question of citizenship. Certainly the electoral act does not put this difficulty in this way. I draw the attention of the committee to clause 45 generally and subsections 4, and on, at page 112. This clause makes it perfectly clear that a person appearing at a poll and seeking the right to vote cannot be required to produce a birth certificate, naturalization papers or anything else. He can be required to swear an affidavit of qualification to vote, in form 43. He is not required to produce the kind of documents we were talking about earlier today.
In short, Canadian citizenship for the purpose of this act is as interpreted by the Canadian Citizenship Act and regulations. In some cases it may involve a difficult combination of law and fact as to whether a person is a Canadian citizen both for the purposes of getting a citizenship certificate and for voting in an election. That matter is not affected either favourably or unfavourably by this bill. It is not affected either way by the stipulations in the Canada Elections Act or in particular by the one we are debating now.

Mr. Chairman, in the preliminary skirmish on this bill and this particular clause, which has consumed a considerable amount of the time of the committee, I indicated that I would propose an amendment. The reason I am disturbed by some of the amendments being proposed is that they are restrictive in their application of the right of the franchise, rather than expansive. Hitherto, in the progress of Canadian democ-

June 22, 1970

racy toward the universal franchise every change that has been made in the Canada Elections Act has been to broaden the base of the voting privilege rather than to narrow that base or to become restrictive in the application of that right.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
The amendment I was thinking of at that time was in the following words, and it is found on page 8259 of Hansard. It is an amendment to subclause 3 of clause 14, and reads as follows:
(3) Every British subject, Commonwealth citizen and citizen of France who has landed immigrant status and who has lived continuously in Canada for a period of one year following the granting of landed immigrant status is deemed to be qualified as an elector.
The thinking at that stage of the debate was that an amendment of this kind would encourage arrivals into Canada to take out landed immigrant status with a view to eventually becoming citizens. Also, as I indicated when we were discussing this matter last Wednesday, I thought that an amendment of this kind would reinforce the values and the traditions which hold the Commonwealth together.
I have been interested to note the comments of the Prime Minister since his return from the Pacific rim tour. He gained a fresh appreciation of the importance and significance of the Commonwealth association. As it has emerged in our modern world, it is an association that has no formal constitutional basis and yet is one of the most meaningful international groupings to be found anywhere in our sadly divided planet. The forces that hold the Commonwealth together are traditions and values that have emerged largely out of the influences that have come from the mother of Parliament at Westminster.
As I listen to the discussions in the House it becomes obvious that the government wants to remove the traditional voting rights of British subjects who are living in Canada, which automatically means that it wants to downgrade the rights and privileges of people coming to Canada who have Commonwealth citizenship status. To my way of thinking this is a retrograde step and, as I have already indicated, it is restrictive rather than expansive.
Another comment that I would like to make is that by broadening the special privileges that have been granted to British subjects and Commonwealth citizens living in Canada, we were encouraging a greater degree of par-

ticipation and involvement in the whole governmental and democratic process. Having listened to the debate, and particularly in light of the amendment which has just been passed by the government majority, I shall have to change my tack somewhat and I will move an amendment to the amended clause 14 by adding to that clause a subclause 4.
During the course of the debate there was some objection to the original form of the amendment that I proposed in that it marked out special classes of people. It seems to me that it is the general sentiment of the House that the time has perhaps come when we might apply the privilege of voting at an earlier stage, on the road to their becoming fully-fledged citizens of Canada, to all new arrivals with landed immigrant status. This is a consummation devoutly to be wished, and certainly it is in tune with the tendency in all previous amendments to the Canada Elections Act to extend the principle of voting universality and put it on a broader base. With this in mind I want to move the addition of the following subclause 4 to clause 14 which, in view of the even more stringent, restrictive amendment put forward by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra-which has just been passed-narrows the voting base almost along the same line as that proposed by the hon. member for Matane. The exception is that it gives it a five-year hoist when the same principle would apply. Therefore, I move the following amendment:
Every person who has landed immigrant status and who has lived continuously in Canada for a period of three years following the granting of landed immigrant status is deemed to he qualified as an elector.
In putting forward this amendment I am aware that the special privilege that was granted to residents of Canada who are British subjects qualified them to vote after one year. Perhaps that is an arbitrary figure, but in light of all the considerations involved in the matter I think at this stage, and in view of the fact that we are making this provision all-inclusive so as to apply to all landed immigrants, the three-year figure would be more appropriate.

Mr. Chairman, I think I originated the other evening, part of the concept herein contained, but for my own part I cannot possibly support the proposition just put forward by my friend the hon. member for Brandon-Souris, for a number of reasons, not the least of which is that it gives to people who are neither Canadian citizens

nor British subjects a preferred class status over and above Canadian citizens and British subjects. As a consequence of the amendment which we have just passed, if British subjects did not become Canadian citizens within five years of the coming into force of the act, they would cease to have the right to vote. The amendment before us simply and unalterably says that every person who has landed immigrant status-which, as I read it, means immigrants from whatever country-and who has lived in Canada for three years shall have forever the right to vote without taking any steps whatever to become a Canadian citizen.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a word on this principle, if I am still in order, so that the public will have knowledge of why a particular point of view is held and why some members of the committee voted as they did on various recommendations. For my part I feel, having listened to the speeches of a number of hon. members, that many hon. members started with the wrong premise. If that was the case, then of course it would be difficult to arrive at the correct conclusion.
Running through the speeches of many hon. members I saw a thread of supposition that the act, as it previously stood, represented a particular privilege so far as English people were concerned. If that were the case I would immediately vote for the elimination of that section from the Canada Elections Act. The concept of this clause is entirely different. I think it is an honourable one to which all fair-minded Canadians could quickly subscribe. The question is whether people who have lived under the same type of democracy that we enjoy, and who are familiar with our parliamentary system of government, should not have the right, on coming to Canada, of exercising the franchise a little sooner than emigrants from a country with an entirely different type of governmental system, even one with a dictatorship. That is the principle which the act tried to designate. In most cases it is a mutual right.
I do not think this right exists because of any international agreement in the Common-

June 22, 1970
Canada Elections Act
wealth. It is one that Canadians enjoy in a number of Commonwealth countries. It is perhaps true that not too many Canadians emigrate to New Zealand, Australia or Great Britain; but a few do, and they would be recognized in those countries as special cases, as persons who had familiarity with the type of parliamentary democracy which is common to most Commonwealth countries. Many members of this House of Commons are members of the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association, which is a body of elected representatives from most of the Commonwealth countries, one of whose aims is to safeguard our common heritage, to try by discussion to solve our common problems and to develop a type of internationalism within the Commonwealth. I think that is an honourable and reasonable aim. But by the action we have taken we are again taking ourselves away from the international association known as the Commonwealth, and we are doing it for what I believe are the wrong reasons. In an age when we should work, wherever practical, toward international understanding we are returning to narrow nationalism.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
Hear, hear!

For that reason I think this amendment, and even the amendment in the bill if it had been left that way, is a retrograde step. I think the amendment moved by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre would have been a slight improvement to the bill, but a number of the other amendments would not.
I regret, Mr. Chairman, that for the wrong reasons we are doing what I believe is the wrong thing. For the reasons I have stated, I would have preferred to have Canadians of whatever background realize that they have this slight advantage, this token advantage of being members of the Commonwealth. The Commonwealth has a common heritage and it is still a force for good in a very confused and chaotic world. Some people would ask what the Commonwealth means. I stand subject to correction, but I do not recall any two Commonwealth countries going to war against each other. It is true that India and Pakistan almost did, but I believe the fact that they were members of a Commonwealth was a restraining influence. It is true that there have been civil wars within the Commonwealth, but I believe it is still a force for good, internationally. Membership should not
[Mr. MacLean.l
only be of benefit to a nation in the international sense, but it should bring benefit to the individual citizens of the Commonwealth.
In the debate some members seemed to indicate that we were giving citizenship to a certain favoured class of people by allowing them to vote. That is not the case. There is no connection between the right to vote and the other privileges of citizenship. These were benefits which Canadians enjoyed and which other countries unilaterally will now take away from Canadians although they may apply in only a few cases. No doubt they will be taken away when we start this trend toward the narrow nationalism which the bill proposes.

Mr. Chairman, I have only one copy of the amendment which I intend to move to subclause 4 because I handed out the copies I had prepared on Tuesday of last week when I wanted to give some prior indication of it to the committee. The sense of my amendment is shown at page 8201 of Hansard for June 16 and it relates to subclause 4 paragraph (e) which reads as follows:
every person undergoing punishment as an inmate in any penal institution for the commission of any offence;
My amendment seeks to remove paragraph (e) from subclause 4. If it is carried, I assume the easy and automatic amendment would be made to the following paragraphs simply by relettering them. I did not put that in the amendment because it is consequential and should flow automatically. I do not anticipate any difficulty in that regard.
The purpose of the amendment is to give people in jail the right to vote in federal elections. Paragraph (g) of subclause 4 would exclude people guilty of corrupt or illegal practices relating to the electoral law. Clause 80 of the bill also covers this category, so that people who have committed an offence against the Elections Act would not have the
June 22. 1970

right to vote, whether or not they were serving time in a penal institution. But all other classes would qualify provided they met the qualifications of being 18 years of age, Canadian citizens or British subjects not disqualified by the five-year rule which the committee has just passed.
I am not sure of the history of the proscription against inmates of penal institutions voting in federal elections. It probably stems from the time when the inmate was totally removed from society and deprived of every vestige of right. There was no concept of parole, rehabilitation or anything of that sort-just the concept of incarceration for the term of his sentence. Once the sentence was served, his rights were reinstated, but during incarceration there was no privilege of correspondence, visiting with friends or anything of an educational or rehabilitative nature. Probably this prohibition in the Elections Act stems from that early approach to penology when inmates of jails were simply forgotten until it became time for their release.
Today we have a more enlightened and generous approach to people who offend against the law. We have the concept of parole, which is a stepping-stone to the complete rehabilitation of the individual. We have the concept of probation and the concept which has just passed this House, of expunging a criminal record after a certain period of time. Within the penitentiary the inmate has the right to correspond with his Member of Parliament and his immediate family and, subject to the approval of officials, to correspond with friends or with a lawyer on legal matters.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
Inmates of penitentiaries can also see television programs brought to them from all over the western world. They learn about the current news and read newspapers and magazines. Inmates of penitentiaries are now given passes which allow them out for two or three days at a time. They may go to the downtown area or elsewhere to look for employment they wish to take up on leaving the penitentiary. There is parole and compassionate leave.
In addition, some inmates before they are released serve the remainder of their time, not on parole but in an institutional structure which in some parts of Canada is a house like many similar houses in the downtown area. An inmate may leave the house, go to work and return to it that night. He is allowed more extended freedom than in jail, and this pre-
Canada Elections Act
pares him for his release. A whole raft of new attitudes is showing up toward inmates of penitentiaries. People are more ready to admit them back into the social stream so that they may participate with the rest of the country in social activities in which the rest of society is engaged.
The purpose of the amendment I am putting forward is primarily rehabilitative. It is to involve the inmate, while he is in jail, in one of the processes of our democracy that deals with a social order of things from which the inmate has dropped out. Because he has become cynical about them and rejected them, he has got into difficulties and landed in jail. I think we ought to take this further step in giving the inmate an opportunity to participate in our electoral process and to choose a Member of Parliament who will have authority and jurisdiction over the penitentiary structure in which the inmate is housed.
I think, secondly, that the mere fact that here we have established a group electors will in itself tend to cause political parties to make a more meaningful determination of penological matters. Candidates would tend more readily to visit penitentiaries in their constituencies. If they did it for no reason except the garnering of votes, something would rub off on them and on the political party they support. Our concepts about penological matters would more truthfully reflect the actual situation in jails. At present we develop our political policies for penitentiary matters in an atmosphere that is far removed from that of the actual prison structure. We seem to develop these policies without really knowing what it is we are developing policies about. Giving inmates a vote would have a secondary effect.
May I draw a parallel. They used to say that the people who were excluded from the vote were people in mental hospitals, those in jail, and Indians. A few years ago we took the Indians off the proscribed list and everyone, including the hon. member for Kamloops-Cariboo, will agree that since then political parties and candidates have paid more attention to Indian people and Indian affairs, even where that has been done for political reasons-and I am not saying that it has been. Actually, I think there was a great deal of altruistic concern about Indians. The point is that candidates and parties began to be more interested in Indian affairs. I think something similar would happen with respect to inmates of penitentiaries.

I know that I ought to have raised this matter before the Standing Committee, but for some reason which escapes my mind at the moment I was not able to appear before the committee and raise it. However, I do not think that should diminish the force of what I am trying to say, and it should not diminish the consideration that the committee will give to this matter.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I move:
That clause 14 be amended by deleting paragraph (e) from subclause 4.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the hon. member would permit a question. I have found his statements extremely interesting. Has he any statistics showing whether similar provisions are in force in other countries in the free world? I hope he will deal with this matter so that we will know whether we are pioneering this sort of thing, or following others.

Mr. Chairman, I can only say this to my hon. friend for Hamilton West. If we are pioneering in this field, good for us. I do not say that personally. If we are following the example of others, if other democratic nations have adopted this course and we are following suit, again I say, good for us. Frankly, I do not know what they are doing in other countries; I have not examined this matter. I have only looked at the situation in Canada. We are revising the Elections Act for the benefit of Canadians, and the Parliament of Canada must deal with the Elections Act. I hope it will also deal with the matter of penitentiaries.
I could find the answer to the hon. gentleman's question very quickly. Later this evening I might consult Mr. Hamel, the Chief Electoral Officer, who may have knowledge of this matter. That is the best way I can answer the hon. gentleman's question. I do not know what is happening in other jurisdictions. I am not too concerned about it because I believe we ought to develop law which is suitable for this country. If such provisions exist in other countries, I say good for them, whether we follow suit, as I hope we shall, or not.
I have discussed this question with Mr. Hamel and with Mr. MacLeod, who was at that time Commissioner of Penitentiaries. He spoke to me shortly before resigning as commissioner. I do not think that lessens the value of What he said to me. I wanted to discuss with these two gentlemen the procedural aspects of this matter as it fell within their respective jurisdictions. Mr. 
Hamel said-I hope I am not misrepresenting our conversation-that there would be no trouble so far as he could see with respect to the procedural aspects of enumeration, revision on election day, etc. As a matter of fact, it might be more easy to enumerate in a penitentiary than in many city communities; the penitentiary authorities would have a fairly accurate record of those qualified to vote.
Unless some were out flooding the rink.
Quite; unless somebody was flooding the skating rink. I think the list of electors would be fairly easy to obtain, even if one or two might not be home, so to speak, at the time of enumeration.

The voters' list is a public document and some people in jail may not want their names to be included on any such public document. Of course, their names no doubt appeared in the newspapers when they were first sent to prison, but most of us hope that these matters are quickly forgotten. Mr. Chairman, I wish to support the proposal of the hon. member for Skeena. However, there are certain technical difficulties in the proposal. I wanted to ask the member some questions to see whether he could help me overcome these difficulties. I agree that the penitentiary system should be a reform and rehabilitation process; therefore, we could give the vote to those who are in peni'entiaries. However, I see real objection to inmates of a penitentiary voting as a group in the constituency wherein the penitentiary is located. These people do not have any real interest in the particular constituency in which they find themselves. They have gone to that constituency for a period of time from other communities. Their homes are in these other communities, their real interest lies there and I do not think it would be fair for several thousand people, as might well be the case, to vote in a constituency in which they had only a temporary interest.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
In Kingston, for example, there are three penitentiaries-Joyceville, Kingston, the women's penitentiary, and maybe even a fourth. I do not think it would be fair for the

people who live in that constituency to have an election decided, perhaps, by individuals who come from other parts of the country. I can visualize the same problem in the St. Vincent de Paul area where there are four penitentiaries. I ask the President of the Privy Council and the hon. member for Skeena whether it might not be possible to consider setting up a system whereby the inmates could vote in their own constituencies under the proxy system, in the same way as members of the armed forces. We have not yet reached the proxy voting clause; it is clause 46 on page 117.
Another possibility would be to strike out subclause 4(f) and leave it up to the penitentiaries authorities to register the inmates through their families in their own constituencies and let them out on parole in order to vote, either on advance polling day or on polling day itself. I do not suggest this could apply to the whole of the prison population, but a certain number could be accommodated in this way. At the present time some inmates are allowed to go home for the weekend to see their families, and others may go home at Christmas and Easter. I am thinking aloud on these matters. If we could work out a system of proxy voting or temporary release to cover the situation, I would be willing to accept the proposal.

speechtext: I suppose my hon. friend from Kingston would want to find out what the attitude of the inmates was to the white paper on taxation before endorsing an idea of that kind. The fact that the commission has on a couple of occasions rejected the concept of an absentee system of balloting prompted me to make my proposal in its present form. I have to deal with the law as it now stands. I, too, have thought about the armed forces voting regulations which give an individual the right to choose whether to register in the constituency in which he is located or in his home constituency wherever that might be. The President of the Privy Council has indicated that it would be possible to adapt those rules for the purpose. He told us that substantial amendments would be required. In any event, it is not impossible to amend the armed forces regulations in this respect. I would not be partial to the idea of leaving it to the head of the institution to determine which inmates should have the opportunity to go home in order to cast their ballots. However meritorious a case might be with regard to a particular inmate, there is always the possibility that he would not desire a three-day pass. The difficulties involved there are such that we ought not to attempt to deal with them.
I can tell the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace that there are many instances in our society where large numbers of people have no particular connection with the constituency in which they are voting though they do, in fact, vote there and perhaps influence the outcome of the election. I have in mind the operations of mining camps, lumber camps, construction camps and the like in remote areas. In my own constituency a good many years ago there was a large-scale construction operation carried out for the Alumium Company of Canada which built a smelter near the community of Kitimat. At the powerhouse site, a whole chain of lakes and rivers was being dammed. The flow of the rivers was being reversed, a tunnel ten miles long was drilled through the mountain, and so on.
It was a massive project involving some 5,000 construction workers in the provincial constituency and, of course, in the federal constituency. They had the opportunity to 22478-43

exercise their right to vote under the provincial and federal law, yet they had no connection whatever with that constituency; they had just gone there to make their stake, after which they went back south or to wherever their homes were. This is the situation in a number of ridings, so I do not think it is a situation which ought to prevent us endorsing the concept I have put forward. Mr. Chairman, I would simply like to say that the only reason which could justify, in my opinion, the wording of subclause 4 (e) of clause 14 would be a technical or practical one.
And how can it be otherwise? Indeed, when we consider that this clause applies to persons imprisoned for minor offences sometimes, and that this can impose a penalty as heavy as the loss of the right to vote, I say that practical reasons alone can explain such a disproportion between the offence and the punishment!
If it is true that the loss of the right to vote is almost the equivalent of civil death, I really would like to know on what grounds someone who is imprisoned for 48 hours, let us say, should lose his right to vote simply because he was in prison at the time of the election.
Even if the reason is a practical one, it does not hold water if we consider that this clause concerns inmates. Let us take the case of someone who is imprisoned for a few years because he has not been able to obtain bail. How will we manage, on election day, to get him to the poll or to his residence? In view of the disproportion between the offence and the penalty, I suggest that the item be allowed to stand so that the legal advisers of the committee of the whole may draft a clause allowing those who are emprisoned to vote. Moreover, I agree with the previous speaker who stated that if the situation of prisoners is so miserable it is because they do not represent a group to be reckoned with during election campaigns.

I therefore propose, in view of the complexity of the practical reasons for the extreme streamlining of Clause 14 (4) (e) it be allowed to stand pending a much more thorough study.

Mr. Chairman, I want to give my views on the amendment proposed by the member for Skeena (Mr. Howard). I would like also to indicate my admiration for his generosity toward those who deliberately have chosen to live on the fringe of society.
However, I cannot approve his attitude since all through his remarks I wondered whether we had not chosen the wrong place. The hon. member has given us such a list of all the advantages granted criminals over the last few years that we may wonder whether it is not more advantageous to live on the fringe of society.
We know how criminals are treated compared to law-abiding citizens. In Canada, thousands of families are living on social welfare. Thousands of workers must live on incomes obviously inadequate and deny themselves things essential to life which prisoners find in penal institutions.
It has been reported not so long ago that the construction of the penal institution at Sainte-Anne-des-Plaines, in the province of Quebec, had cost $32,000 per inmate. However, thousands of Canadian families have to live in slum dwellings which do not even belong to them and in distressing conditions, while $32,000 is available to accomodate individuals who did not want to comply with Canadian laws.
In my opinion, if we grant these people the right to choose members of Parliament, we are giving in to them a little too much.
Moreover, a comparison was established between members of the armed forces and prisoners. This is stupid. No comparison should be drawn between those who defend their country and those who destroy it. If we give prisoners the franchise, we must give it to saboteurs and traitors also.
On these grounds, I cannot support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Skeena. The hon. member for Matane (Mr. De Bane) who spoke before me is wondering what would happen in the case of a man sentenced to 48 hours in jail at the very time of an election. I would answer him that when somebody is sentenced to 48 hours in jail, the offence is not likely to be a crime but rather some petty larceny or some minor offence.

Moreover, I am sure that in such a case, a Canadian judge would have enough understanding to defer the sentence.
I do not think the present Elections Act aims at granting the right to vote to those who have deliberately chosen to be outcasts. If we make it easier for those people than for those who are law abiding citizens, I am afraid we shall have to change sides.
Such are the reasons why I cannot support the amendment of the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard).

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the merits of the amendment moved by the member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) are not easy to ascertain and, consequently, must not be taken lightly.
I believe our society now accepts the concept whereby citizens who break the law of the land are not condemned to prison to suffer any other penalty than that of being deprived of their freedom. And so, citizens who are imprisoned do not suffer any corporal punishments which ar spumed by our laws. Citizens who now break the law and are imprisoned are not, generally speaking, deprived of access to information. In fact, they have access to literature and information.
Therefore, such citizens as are imprisoned are merely deprived of their freedom of movement. And even there, practise has it that more and more the prisoners are given the right to leave the institution for short spells at regular intervals. The citizen is therefore to be rehabilitated instead of being completely removed from the normal environment, so that he might readjust himself to society after serving his term.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
I therefore ask myself two things with regard to the amendment proposed by the member for Skeena: First of all, whether the prisoners are well-informed; and secondly, whether they can have the will to improve society. Indeed, that is how, generally speaking, I understand franchise. Now, because in practice prisoners are given instead of denied access to information through radio programs, television, newspapers, they are in a position to follow the evolution of society like all other citizens, to see how the affairs of the state are managed, and so to pass judgment. Does the fact that he is excluded from normal life constitute a valid reason for denying him the right to vote?
June 22, 1970

Considering the information, I do not think so, for to admit that the fact of being cut off somewhat from the normal life of the political society to which we belong could result in being deprived of one's right to vote should lead us normally to the same way of thinking as regards servicemen stationed abroad. Servicemen, to whom we recognize the right to vote, do not live in their normal social environment, do not live within our frontiers. In order to get the necessary information and be able to have a sound opinion as to the administration of public affairs, they must rely on the mass media as a whole. This goes to say that their means of getting information are not better than those of an inmate within prison walls.
Moreover, can a prisoner feel a real desire to improve society, which would be the normal consequence of the exercise of his franchise?
I believe first of all that the prisoner, if he is married, surely wants his family to live in society as he sees it: the best possible for his children, for his wife, for his friends and for the community as a whole. Can the fact that he committed a crime or an offense prevent him from giving his opinion on the rights we constantly deal with during our sessions, the rights affecting the life of every citizen, whatever was his behaviour in society?
And I do not think so. If we really believe in the way we apply the rules in our penitentiaries, if we sincerely believe that a criminal should be rehabilitated, we should give him the right to give his opinion on the kind of society that will be established and the kind of people who will administer it on his behalf.
This is why I would have liked it better had the amendment moved by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) mentioned one exception, namely life-term prisoners because they cannot hope to lead ever a normal life in society.
I think that a life-term prisoner should lose his franchise. It would be an exception.
I think that we should welcome the amendment moved by the hon. member for Skeena since, in general, it meets two concepts which are really the basis of the franchise: first, to properly inform the prisoner so that he may exercice his right to vote in an enlightened manner and on the other hand, his actual desire to improve society and to put it in the hands of responsible men.

Mr. Chairman, I am not going to give all my views on criminology or penology, but I think it would be wise if this suggestion were given a good deal more reflection, perhaps a good deal more than that suggested by the hon. member for Matane. I think there are many things we ought to reflect upon.
The suggestion which the hon. member tossed out was one which shook me rigid, to use the vernacular. The authorities of the institutions would make the decision as to which group would vote on advance polling and which would vote on election day. It seems to me this would call upon them to make a qualitative judgment which I would not ask them to make even if they were a college of archangels. The success of that venture would be very problematical.
I am a little concerned, too, about the ethical problems as distinct from some of the legal problems. The mover of the amendment would exclude from voting, shall we say, someone who gave a voter a bottle of rum on election day, but someone who gave half a dozen voters a Molotov cocktail would be all right for ever and a day under this proposal. There may be a lot of ethical judgments which we will have to reflect upon as we look into this interesting suggestion.
Going through my mind has been the question which always has been difficult in elections, namely, what is meant by "ordinary residence"? When I apply that concept to this amendment, I am equally concerned about what is ordinary residence. I have a feeling that the administrative problems as to the location of the institutions are pretty complex. I am still a little concerned about the posting of the names. society. It seems to me that if we accept some of the suggestions put forward by the hon. member who proposed this amendment, we will make our society permissive to the point of extreme exaggeration.
With regard to the fact that there are people in jail for minor offences, may I respectfully point out that they would not be there if they had obeyed the law. However, in addition to that the hon. member is suggesting that rapists, murderers, arsonists and people who commit treason should have the right to vote. May I point out to you, Mr. Chairman, that people who disobey the laws of Canada and disobey the laws of Parliament should lose some of the rights which they had in our society.
I am not saying that I am against these people being allowed to see their families, because our law allows it. But I point out that they receive excellent board and lodging free of charge, paid for by the taxpayers of Canada. They are rehabilitated and reformed to the best of our ability. Yet here tonight there are hon. members who suggest that prisoners who have been in jail for a long time, and who perhaps will be there for a long time in the future because they have committed a crime, whether it be murder or rape of our wife or our daughter, should have the same rights as people who live in the rural communities, the towns, villages and cities of Canada.
I will not take any longer except to say that there is one way in which they can get the vote, and that is to obey the law. That fact should be stressed right across this country of ours. 1 appreciate that when these people are on parole, they should have the right to vote. That is fine, because society and the authorities concerned say they are safe to be out on the street and they are being rehabilitated to the best of our ability. But when they are in jail for having committed a hideous crime- and it has even been suggested tonight that they may have the right to run for Parliament and be elected-I say that is going too far. This amendment, so far as our being a permissive society is concerned, goes much too far for my taste.

Mr. Chairman, I am certain that the hon. gentleman who preceded me must be referring to permissive society in another context than the one I consider we now have. The way in which he has approached this subject would make our society a sick society-and this is exactly what we are facing today. Those who are 
supporting this amendment to give the right to vote to inmates of penitentiaries are not asking for charity. All we are asking for is the inmates' rehabilitation.
Whether or not the hon. member who preceded me has visited many penitentiaries and spoken to many of their inmates is, of course, for him to tell us. I suggest that if we are to have an enlightened society we must consider proposals such as the one that is before us. If we as politicians and legislators are concerned about creating an enlightened society, we must develop a social conscience and look at the whole situation.
I appreciate-many hon. members have suggested this tonight-that the provisions of this amendment may be difficult to enforce at times, but we as legislators should insert in the law the principle we believe should be in it; the mechanics of enforcing it can easily be applied later. I am sure that the people who drafted this legislation can look after that area. Some hon. members have said we should not give the right to vote to inmates of penitentiaries. I suggest that on speaking to these people one finds that they are much more enlightened than many people who have not served a prison sentence. I suggest that people who have served a prison term have paid their debt to society, so why should we ask them to pay a second debt? They were sentenced by a judge who decided they must pay a debt to society. It is time we decided not to impose a double penalty on them.
It is very easy for the hon. member who preceded me to use the tone of voice he did and to say that these people should be taken out of society. But it is not the idea of penal institutions to rehabilitate them? As one reads "The Rise and Fall of the Third Reich" one is reminded of the previous speaker when he spoke of rehabilitation. I suggest that if we as legislators have the will power to try to improve society, then we should improve our whole society by taking into consideration those people who are within the walls of penitentiaries. I am sure that ours does not have to be a permissive society, but rather a just society-and not in the terms used on many occasions by the Prime Minister. I refer to a society with a social conscience and a realization that people within penitentiary walls are paying a debt to society and should not have the right to vote taken away from them.

I have no desire to seek revenge on those who have no feeling for society, but I cannot quite see how we can give the vote to people who are guilty of treason, arson, aggravated assault, rape, armed robbery or murder. The greatest privilege that a Canadian can enjoy, next to that of life, is the right to vote in free elections. We should use it as a lever to encourage these people to get back into productive society.

The present law is very broad and would allow a man on parole to have full voting rights and all the other privileges of a citizen. Having worked with the Parole Board, I know that it is making every effort to return prisoners to productive society as soon as possible, bearing in mind the importance of protecting society. Next to wanting their liberty, self-respecting prisoners may want the right to vote. This very fact may be an encouragement to some of them to see the error of their ways. Mr. Chairman, members of the committee would be correct in thinking me prejudiced when I say that the hon. member for Skeena presented his amendment and his case in the most reasoned manner we have heard in this chamber on any amendment to this bill. Whether one agrees or disagrees with his argument, I believe all of us were impressed by the fact that he keeps hitting certain areas. I wondered whether he had intended to do that and I believe other members of the committee were wondering the same. In the course of his argument he in fact covered many areas of problem and difficulty, whether they be administrative or economic.
I support the amendment of the hon. member for a number of reasons which I shall mention later. First, I ask this question of myself and of my colleagues in the committee: What are we afraid of? We know that in every election there are thousands of people who do not vote, but no matter how picayune their reasons we do not lose any sleep over it unless we think we have a chance of winning by appeal or recount. If we pass this amendment, probably 10,000 or 12,000 people across Canada will be eligible to cast a ballot in a federal election. It is probable that many of them will not choose to be enumerated and to vote, as do many civilians.
It is suggested that those who have broken the law should pay the full penalty, and upon return to civilian life should have the rights and privileges of ordinary citizenship returned to them. With due deference to hon. members, if that argument has any validity Mr. Chairman, I suggest it follows that those who break the law but are not in penitentiaries should be deprived of the right to cast a ballot. Those who get away with extorsion, with usury, phony bankruptcies, even closing-

out sales or high rents, commit crimes just as hideous in civilian society-but they have the full right of the franchise.
I am sure we all agree that the purpose of our electoral law and this amendment is to maximize the opportunity of Canadians to cast their ballot. Given that principle, our objective should be to enlarge the opportunity of the maximum number of people in this country to cast their ballot. Of course there will be administrative difficulties. For a moment I hoped that the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace would support our amendment. He did not let me down: he told us how well he thought of it, and then gave us all the reasons why it cannot be done. Of course there will be administrative problems, but I have faith in the Chief Electoral Officer and the prison officials and I believe the problems can be solved.
What the committee needs to be concerned with is whether inmates of institutions should have the opportunity to cast a ballot. Some of them will be permanent residents and some will be there only a short time, but the day the enumeration starts they will be "ordinarily resident" because any prison term over two years is served in a penitentiary. These really are not problems: they may be excuses to avoid making the essential decision of whether inmates should be entitled to the franchise. Of course, there could be a block of this type of vote in some constituencies, and if they were to vote the same way they could elect their chosen candidate. But what else is new, Mr. Chairman? I suspect this could happen with civilian electors in a score of constituencies in Canada where a block of votes in one direction could swing the election. If we were to worry about the problem, we probably would have no electoral laws, because we all know that we make appeals to blocks of voters of various ethnic or social origins.

If we include the inmates of penitentiaries within our electoral system, we might develop better penal laws than we have at the moment. I think those who are worried have no valid worry. I suggest the first thing we ought to consider is that inmates are human beings, no matter how inhuman might have been their actions at some time; second, they are citizens of Canada; third-this point was mentioned earlier-it seems to me that we should begin a small process which would lead to the rehabilitation of many of those in

penal institutions. If we accomplish that, what have we lost? Surely that chance is worth taking, both for the sake of the inmates and for society as a whole.
Some hon. members are worried in case an inmate of a jail becomes a candidate. It has been known to happen that a person in jail has been elected to office. I am thinking of John Queen-I think that is his name-when serving a jail term was elected to the Manitoba legislature in 1920 or 1921. I do not know how he was let out of jail. I understand that he walked across the street from the jail to the legislature and took his seat. There is also Louis Riel who was under the shadow of a jail term when he was elected to this House. He served in this House for one day and then stole across the river in the dark to a neighbouring country and fled west. Doubtless we could find other examples if we were to study Canadian history.
In any event, I do not understand why anyone need worry because I would be very surprised if any of the political parties represented in this House nominated as a candidate any inmate of a penal institution. Second, if such a man were ever nominated I suspect ways and means could be found of permitting him to sit here, even if a guard had to sit beside him in the House. Third, and perhaps this is the most important part of my argument, if we permit inmates of penitentiaries to vote, when we come to the appropriate clause of the bill an hon. member could move an amendment which would prohibit inmates serving prison terms from being candidates at elections.
I emphasize that it is most important for us to maximize the franchise. We are not considering a large group of voters, perhaps only 10,000 or 12,000. That, I should think, is not really the point. I think the real point is-I shall not belabour it-that here we have an opportunity to take one more step in the right direction in our modern and, I hope, increasingly more civilized society. We need to make an effort on behalf of those who are in penitentiaries. It seems to me that if we obtain some response from them for our effort, we shall be rewarded. No matter whether our efforts works or not, we shall know that we have tried. I submit to hon. members that our trying cannot harm the electoral process, the Canadian society or democracy. It may not do any good, but I do not know that and neither does anyone else. I think we ought to try because no matter how small our reward is, it will be worth it.
One could try to reply to the hon. member for Bruce and those who feel as he does, but one might lose his temper and not contribute much to the debate which so far has been rather bipartisan and multipartisan on this extremely important bill. If all the restrictions and penalties in the penal laws of Canada and of other nations-I say this with particular reference to those we have repealed-were so good, why did they not work? We accept that our amendment will not solve all the problems; neither will it turn inmates of penitentiaries automatically into fine, upright citizens, although some of them are at least as upright and upstanding as many who are loose in society. But I think it will help. I hope that without taking up much more time on the question the committee will say, "Yes, why not? Let us try it. Let us make our little contribution and try to return these people to society." I think if we do that, in a few years time we shall be glad we did.

Mr. Chairman, our friends of the NDP, so as to seem progressive, are trying to defy all those who live on the fringe of society and who are against it.
I am in favour of the rehabilitation of inmates. But to give them the right to vote goes against a principle of society to the effect that criminals accept beforehand to be deprived of their civic rights.
When I see our friends of the NDP trying to "deify" all kind of people who run counter to the principles of society and the law, I wonder whether they are sincere or whether they are merely trying to play politics.
I have nothing against inmates, but they must show that they are capable of rehabilitation before they are liberated. That is why I maintain that the proposed amendment goes too far. That we should give the right to vote to a prisoner on parole, I have nothing against that. But an individual who has served a sentence of ten or fifteen years, who has never shown a desire to rehabilitate himself and who has appeared several times before a court of justice cannot lay claim to the same civic rights as those who obey the law.
My hon. friends of the New Democratic party are too anxious to deify those persons who, besides, have all my sympathy. If they have perpetrated indictable offences against society, they must bear the consequences of their actions and be deprived of their civil rights.

Mr. Chairman, some of the objections raised in regard to the amendment of the hon. member for Skeena were the administrative difficulties which might arise if we voted for it and allowed inmates of a penitentiary to vote. I wish to explain to the House that we can vote in favour of this proposal and still have a system whereby inmates will be allowed to vote in their own constituencies. I have already pointed out that under the section "residence", we can provide that an inmate can vote in the residence with his family or at his last listed address.
Hear, hear!

When we come to the part on proxy voting, to complement what I have already said I will move an amendment to clause 46, subclause 1 in which I will add a paragraph (d) with the words "his detention in a penal institution". In addition to students being allowed to vote by proxy if they are resident at a university, inmates in a penal institution will be included. These inmates will be able to use the proxy voting procedure to vote in the electoral district of their family or, if they have no family, at their last listed address. As I said, I will vote in favour of this amendment for the reasons I have just put forward. I have listened to the speeches in this debate. Many members say we should not give the vote to those who have committed a crime and are in penitentiaries, because they deserve to lose that privilege. That is a vindictive and punitive approach to prison reform.
Hear, hear!

The whole purpose of a penitentiary system should be that when people leave the penitentiary they are better-prepared citizens than they were when they entered. If the penitentiary system means that

I will be very brief because I know it is the disposition of the committee to vote on this amendment. I do not want to delay the vote. I will only comment fleetlingly on what other members have said, including the hon. member for Charlevoix. I point out to him and other hon. members that regardless of what they may think-and I do not have to overemphasize this-this proposition was put forward by me as an individual. It was not put forward by the New Democratic Party, nor do the great bulk of the members of my party agree with this concept of rehabilitation. It was put forward in all sincerity. It did not call for the unkind remarks that were made.
I wish to refer briefly to the subject of rehabilitation. I hope it will have some effect on those hon. members who feel they should not support the proposition and should retain the punitive nature of the treatment of people in our prisons. We have tried all sorts of repressive measures such as heavy sentences, classing people as habitual criminals, removing their rights, and so on. None of these has worked in any measurable way. In our penitentiaries four out of five inmates have been in jail before. Only in recent years has our penitentiary system been altered. An alteration occurred as a result of the Parliament of Canada expressing the idea that we should be less rigid and confining and that we should concern ourselves with the fact that people in penitentiaries are human beings worthy of consideration, and not merely numbers.
Rehabilitation is not measurably affected by the conditions in a jail. It does not matter whether they are painted different colours, whether they have toilet facilities or what the situation may be. Rehabilitation is a state of mind on the part of an individual, a desire on his part to alter his attitude toward society and a desire to think truthfully and honestly about himself. If we can offer him one small fragment of an opportunity to face the truth about himself and his rehabilitation while he is in jail undergoing punishment, if we can let him participate in our democratic society while he is there, it will be for his good. He will have an opportunity to reflect on what he is doing and on what society is doing. It will be another step toward rehabilitating the individual to being a complete human being and a full citizen.

That subclause 4 be amended by inserting the following as paragraph (h): "that the members of the Senate of Canada be listed among those disqualified."
This is not the outpouring of one who is against the Senate. On the contrary, I am one who lives in the hope that some day I may become a member of that illustrious body. As I tell the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, when I reach the age of 74J I shall support his persistent motion to abolish the Senate, but until then I shall not.
There has always been the closest possible correlation between eligibility for candidacy and voting rights. Then again, people who are themselves members of a particular body do not vote to decide who are to become members of that body. In this sense I believe the Senate of Canada has not received the respect which it deserves. Its members are already represented in this Parliament as being members of the red chamber. It often happens that the word "Parliament" is used with reference only to those of us who are members of the green chamber. The Americans fall into the same error when they speak of congressmen; they are speaking, really, only of members of the House of Representatives. There is, of course, the British precedent that members of the House of Lords may not vote for candidates for the House of Commons-and I have recently come to think that the British know quite a bit about electioneering.
I believe we enhance respect for the Senate, to which body I hope to win my way some time, by recognizing that its members are in

maintopic: POLLUTION-MONITORING OF WATERS RECEIVING EFFLUENT DISCHARGES FROM PLANTS USING MERCURY
POLLUTION-MONITORING OF WATERS RECEIVING EFFLUENT DISCHARGES FROM PLANTS USING MERCURY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 10 I asked the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Davis) the following question:
Is the Fisheries Department monitoring all those waters in Canada which receive effluent discharges from industrial plants using mercury processes in their operations? If so, how many such monitoring operations are currently under way?
[DOT] (11:10 p.m.)
Mercury pollution has become a major threat to many of our lakes and rivers. It apparently has been with us for a long period of time, but was never detected because no adequate tests for it were carried out. We now find that it has reached into Hudson Bay, where rather severe mercury contamination has been found in beluga whalemeat. The contamination must have come from the Nel-son-Saskatchewan River and it is thought that it originated from chemical plants in Saskatoon and in Dryden, Ontario. This means that hundreds of miles of a very large river and of a large lake in Manitoba must have been severely contaminated, because the fish and eventually the whales in Hudson Bay, have been affected. A similar story will probably unfold in other areas of Canada. Mercury poisoning is prevelant in Howe Sound in British Columbia, where it has forced closure of one of the finest sports fishing areas in the province. We have had the Saskatchewan River closed for months, at great cost to the Canadian taxpayers. Lake St. Clair has been closed to commercial fishing, and parts of the Ottawa River have also been closed.
Mercury is used in many major industries. Its use in fungicides is well known, and this use has been the source of some serious mercury pollution problems. Its compounds are useful in manufacturing and are used in some paints to prevent mildewing. The largest users of mercury are the electrical equipment industry and the manufacturers of chlorine and caustic soda. It is used as a catalyst in a
June 22, 1970

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion number of chemical manufacturing processes, particularly in the manufacture of vinyl chloride which is the base of many plastics. Mercury and its compounds can accumulate and be concentrated in living things. In this respect it is similar to radioactive pollution and to some pesticides such as DDT. Mercury in water is picked up and concentrated by fish. Birds and other species of sea life may further concentrate the mercury by eating contaminated fish. This is why any source of mercury pollution is dangerous.
I understand that some pulp factories used a mercury compound called phenyl mercury acetate-PMA

to prevent the growth of slime from fungi which clogs machines, and they discharge this PMA with their waste water. I do not know if any of our Canadian pulp plants use this mercury compound, but it should be checked out by the government. I have mentioned the chloralkali plants which produce chlorine and caustic soda by electrolytic process. The heaviest concentration of these plants is along the St. Lawrence River. Have all these plants been checked, along with the water, the river bottom and the fish in the vicinity of the plants? Has the department a list of all the industrial plants in Canada using mercury processes, and have these plants been checked to determine if a mercury pollution problem could exist in their operations? Does the department have sufficient research staff to carry out the monitoring required when a pollution problem is suspected?
These are important and urgent questions. I trust that the minister will be able to give us an assurance that the problem of mercury pollution is not only being looked into but that any offending industrial plant has been forced to take measures to rectify and prevent any further pollution from this source.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jack Davis (Minister of Fisheries and Forestry):
maintopic: POLLUTION-MONITORING OF WATERS RECEIVING EFFLUENT DISCHARGES FROM PLANTS USING MERCURY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding) has asked several questions. The first is: Does the fisheries department monitor all those waters in Canada which receive effluent discharged from industrial plants using mercury processes in their operation? The answer is yes. The major industries using mercury, which previously were discharging substantial amounts of mercury into the waters of Canada, are the chloralkali industries, the chemical processing industries making caustic soda and chlorine principally for the pulp and paper industry, and the pulp and paper

industry itself. There are 12 such chloralkali plants in Canada.
We have had meetings in Ottawa with all the plants involved. We have monitored all the waters downstream of those plants where we know there has been a degree of mercury contamination in those waters. Steps have been taken, either directly by the federal Department of Fisheries or in conjunction with the provincial departments administering the Fisheries Act, to close local fisheries where mercury levels were high, to compensate fishermen, to identify areas of the river bottom which were contaminated with mercury and to arrange for them to be dredged out. The answer to the difficulties in the chloralkali industry has been total recirculation of the mercury effluent within the plant systems. This has been arranged in all cases.
We have also had meetings in Ottawa with representatives of the pulp and paper industry. There are approximately 140 pulp and paper mills in this country. A majority of them in years gone by used fungicides containing mercury. Progressively they have stopped using these fungicides, mainly because their customers require products which could not possibly contain mercury of any kind. However, at the beginning of 1970 there were still six pulp and paper mills in this country using these fungicides. Their use has since been discontinued.
We have been monitoring the waters downstream of those and other mills which were known within the last decade to use fungicides containing mercury. HEALTH AND WELFARE-INCLUSION OF OPTOMETRIC SERVICES UNDER MEDICARE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject I want to discuss tonight has been under discussion off and on in this House for the past four years. I raised it again on June 17 when I directed a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro). It seemed that in reply the minister was opening the door and that at long last we were going to get a definitive response to the question of including paramedical services, particularly optometric
June 22, 1970

services, under the medicare act. It is not necessary, nor do I have the time, to review the chequered experience in pursuing this matter when the medicare bill was before the House. Members became concerned over the possible application of paramedical services. At that time an amendment was moved which indicated that upon the request of a province, paramedical services could be included. Again, because of the widespread interest in optometric services it was specifically mentioned.
The reason optometric services are a matter of great concern to many hon. members is that this is the only eye care service available to large numbers of people who live outside the larger urban centres. We are all aware that there is a shortage of ophthalmological services. This means that if Canadians in our rural communities are to receive even the basic refraction tests and are to be covered by the medicare program, which is supposed to be a universal program, they must depend upon the services of optometrists who serve in our smaller communities.
I asked the minister whether it was his intention, based on the fact that a consensus has been reached by the provinces participating in the program, that the government of Canada will now recognize the principle established in the amendment and cover optometric services under the medicare act.
[DOT] (11:20 p.m.)
The minister replied that there was to be a meeting during the summer, within the coming two months, with the provincial health ministers at which time the subject would be considered, and that the provincial government concerned would again be canvassed for a consensus. The uncertainty arises from this concept of consensus. It was not present at all in the original amendment. As a matter of fact, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) specifically raised this point and got an answer from the then Minister of Health and Welfare that it would apply when a single province asked for this particular coverage for its citizens.

INDUSTRY-PROPOSED CLOSING OP CANADIAN SUBSIDIARY BY SKIL CORPORATION OF CHICAGO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like first of all to say that I am pleased the minister is here this evening to reply to my question. I trust that whatever sleep he loses tonight he will be able to catch up on tomorrow, either in his office or some other appropriate place.
The battle for Canadian control of our economy is coming to a boil, perhaps even to a brawl. It began to simmer even before the ill-fated budget of Walter Gordon and precipitated the decline of Mr. Gordon, a once powerful force in the Liberal cabinet, to his final isolation and resignation just before the last election. It seems that Mr. Grodon was no longer credible with his colleagues, in spite of the fact that the Watkins report on the subject of the tremendous foreign inroads-and by that I mean United States inroads-that had been made in our economy had been tabled in the meantime.
The Watkins report of 1964 cited, fearfully, large percentages of foreign ownership in some industries, notably gas, oil, mining and autos, and suggested that it might be too late for Canada ever again to regain control of her economy. "So what", many were heard to say, "Hasn't every developing country needed foreign investment at the start? Haven't Canadians the second highest standard of living in the world? What difference does it really make, anyway, who owns what as long as our resources are developed and employment is provided our citizens? And don't we need not less, but even more foreign capital?"
This view, of course, I believe has been the view accepted by most Canadians who have thought about the matter at all. Indeed it is the position that must have been taken by the Liberal government, because to my knowledge not one new piece of legislation was initiated to protect us from foreign takeovers as a result of Professor Watkins' 1964 study. Lately the people of Canada have been making slightly different sounds and there has been a resurgence of concern over such issues. "Sure, we enjoy a high standards of living," some are saying, "but is it really worth it if the price tag includes polluting our waters by pulp mills and decimating our wildlife ranges with open coal pits?"


The government has at last reacted. That is what governments always do-they seldom act; they only react. We are now seeing what amounts to a government flip-flop on the question of Canadian nationalism. The sale of our Mercantile Bank to the New York City Bank was forbidden, as was the proposed sale by Denison uranium mines to foreign interests more recently. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) introduced a bill to assert sovereignty over Canada's Arctic. The Minister of Energy (Mr. Greene) formerly regarded as a continentalist, reversed himself in Denver last month and became instead a sabre-rattling chauvinist, even going so far as to suggest jamming the air waves to protect us from United States' cultural imperialism.
All these things may be the result of government rethinking and enlightenment, and they are fine even though far off and remote from the concerns of the average Canadian worker. To get closer to my home and the subject that we are debating tonight, the importance of Canadian ownership is very real to 125 wage earners in the lower mainland of British Columbia. In 1968 a local firm, Power Machinery, was purchased by the multinational corporation Skil, the saw people of Chicago. My correspondents tell me that Skil now wants to close down its Vancouver operation on the ground of surplus production capacity in Chicago. What might happen- and I know of no present law to prevent its happening-is that the lower mainland of B.C. will be deprived of 125 jobs in order that Chicago can gain the same number. This small, local example has been replicated hundreds of times all over the country during recent years. Where are the former foods canneries of the Fraser Valley? What is to become of the 600 Dunlop workers recently laid off in Toronto?
This process of rationalization in order to maximize the advantages of the multinational corporation makes good economic sense to the corporation, but makes no sense at all to the men who are about to be unemployed. For that matter, what economic advantage can accrue to this country as the result of such policies? This is the nub of the problem of foreign ownership. It is not that Americans are sinister people who have taken advantage of us-quite the opposite; it is that Canadians, through their government, have encouraged this trend and thus vital decisions regarding Canada's future continue to be made beyond our borders.

Up to now, as tar as I know there has been no legal way for us to stop the sell-out habit.
I think from the context of what I have said the question I am enlarging upon tonight needs no repetition. The minister knows whereof I speak. I conclude by saying that I hope the reply of the minister will give these job holders some hope. I can understand if the Skil Corporation in their corporate wisdom decide to pull out of the B.C. operation. Perhaps the minister will tell us what his intentions are and what he may be able to do legally. Fine words are very tremendous and very comforting for a time. I do not think anyone would dispute the fact that Canada has no legal means of protecting the Canadian worker from this kind of pull-out. I am aware that the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce has been in touch with the company officials-probably with its usual kind of genial persuasiveness, if I know the minister. My intervention tonight is made in the hope that we can keep this issue alive. The minister might indicate some positive steps, and I look forward to hearing his reply.
